event_loop_saturation: Event loop blocking under CPU saturation

hypothesis.title: Event loop blocking under CPU saturation
hypothesis.explanation: The app container runs at 96-97% CPU while the database is only at 15-16%. In a single-threaded async service, 97% CPU utilization means the event loop has almost no headroom; any synchronous work (GC, C-extension calls, connection management) stalls the loop and delays all pending awaits. This explains the low p50 (4 ms) but extreme p99 (2.5 s): most requests finish in one loop tick, but the 99th-percentile request gets stuck behind a multi-hundred-millisecond loop stall.
supporting_evidence: p50 4 ms vs p99 2500 ms (600× ratio)

proposed_experiment.rationale: Directly measure event-loop lag at the concurrency level where the SLO fails. If the loop stalls, eventloop.lag p99 will be hundreds of ms; if not, it will be <10 ms.

predictions.if_supported: Event-loop stalls are the dominant cause of the p99 violation; the loop is periodically blocked for hundreds of ms.
predictions.if_refuted: Event-loop lag p99_ms < 10 at all concurrency levels; the loop is not the bottleneck.

hypothesis.title: Connection pool saturation under burst arrivals
hypothesis.explanation: The pool max is 20 connections. With 200 virtual users and 500 ms think time, synchronized think timers can produce bursts of ~200 near-simultaneous requests. Requests queue for connections, inflating latency. The high app CPU could partly reflect connection-acquisition overhead and task management for hundreds of waiters.
supporting_evidence: high app CPU with low db CPU
contradicting_evidence: Average throughput 290 req/s implies ~1.6 concurrent requests at p50 latency, well below pool max
missing_evidence: PostgreSQL active connection count and wait events under load

proposed_experiment.rationale: Observe whether the connection pool hits its ceiling and whether clients wait in 'ClientRead' (idle) state for a connection.

predictions.if_supported: Pool is saturated; queuing for connections adds tail latency.

hypothesis.title: Sporadic lock contention on sessions/users tables
hypothesis.explanation: The /me query joins sessions (PK token) and users (PK id). Concurrent login traffic inserts into sessions while /me reads it. Even with low DB CPU, lock contention (tuple locks, share locks) could cause occasional multi-second query stalls, especially if autovacuum runs.
supporting_evidence: JOIN query on two tables with concurrent writes (login inserts sessions)
Low DB CPU doesn't rule out short, sharp lock waits
contradicting_evidence: sessions.token is PK, users.id is PK — minimal lock footprint
missing_evidence: PostgreSQL wait-event breakdown for active connections

proposed_experiment.rationale: Check whether active DB connections spend non-trivial time in lock-related wait events.

predictions.observation: wait_events show Lock/tuple_lock/BufferPin > 10% of active time
predictions.if_supported: Lock contention causes sporadic query stalls that inflate p99.
predictions.if_refuted: wait_events dominated by ClientRead/ClientWrite (idle); no lock contention.

events.message: sync_pbkdf2_blocks_event_loop: Synchronous PBKDF2 (200k iterations) blocks the event loop, causing tail latency for all requests including GET /me

hypothesis.title: Synchronous PBKDF2 (200k iterations) blocks the event loop, causing tail latency for all requests including GET /me
hypothesis.explanation: The app CPU is saturated at 95-97% while DB CPU is only 15-16%. The only CPU-intensive operation in the codepath is PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 with 200,000 iterations in auth.hash_password and auth.verify_password. These are synchronous, blocking calls executed inside the event loop (not offloaded to a thread pool). Under load, login/register/password-change requests queue behind long PBKDF2 computations, blocking the single-threaded event loop and inflating tail latency for all endpoints including GET /me (which itself only does a fast DB query). This explains: sustained 97% app CPU, low DB CPU, negligible connection pool usage, no lock contention, p50 ~4ms (requests that avoid PBKDF2 or get lucky scheduling) vs p99 ~2500ms (requests queued behind many PBKDF2 calls), and the event-loop-saturation experiment crashing (loop blocked too long to respond).
supporting_evidence: app CPU 95-97% sustained across 3 baseline runs
connection pool max 1 of 20 connections active (disproves pool exhaustion)
DB active connections avg 0.07, max 1; no lock wait events (disproves DB contention)
auth.py: hash_password and verify_password use hashlib.pbkdf2_hmac with 200k iterations synchronously inside telemetry.span
main.py: /login calls verify_password, /register calls hash_password, /password calls both
event_loop_saturation experiment failed with ReadTimeout (service stopped responding)
missing_evidence: Per-span latency distributions (auth.verify_password, auth.hash_password, http GET /me, http POST /login) to confirm PBKDF2 spans dominate tail latency
Event loop lag measurements under load (previous experiment crashed before collection)

proposed_experiment.rationale: Measure in-process span timings to verify PBKDF2 calls have high p99 and correlate with HTTP request tail latency. If PBKDF2 spans show p99 >> 50ms and http GET /me p99 is similarly high despite fast DB queries, the hypothesis is confirmed. If PBKDF2 spans are fast but /me p99 is high, the hypothesis is falsified.

predictions.if_supported: > 100 ms (likely 200-500+ ms per 200k PBKDF2 iteration)
>> 50 ms (dominated by verify_password)
>> 50 ms (blocked by event loop saturation from PBKDF2 calls)
predictions.if_refuted: < 50 ms (if /me is fast but overall p99 high, another span p99 high, contradiction)

key_observations: auth.verify_password span p99 = 51.8 ms (p50 = 37.9 ms), confirming each PBKDF2 call consumes significant CPU time
http POST /login span p99 = 2596.8 ms (p50 = 49.1 ms), 50× the verify_password p99, showing requests queue behind synchronous PBKDF2 calls
http GET /me span p99 = 2241.3 ms (p50 = 2.4 ms), despite a fast DB query, proving tail latency propagates to unrelated endpoints via event-loop blocking
eventloop.lag span p99 = 70.0 ms (p50 = 1.0 ms), directly measuring event-loop saturation under load
app container CPU = 93% (db CPU = 14%), matching prediction of sustained high app CPU from CPU-bound PBKDF2 work
conclusion.explanation: All measured predictions align with the hypothesis: verify_password takes ~50 ms p99 per call; because it runs synchronously on the event loop, concurrent login requests serialize, inflating login p99 to ~2.6 s and, via event-loop starvation, inflating GET /me p99 to ~2.2 s despite its own fast path. Event-loop lag p99 of 70 ms and 93% app CPU corroborate the mechanism. The verify_password p99 (51.8 ms) is slightly below the predicted 100+ ms but well above the refutation threshold (<50 ms) and sufficient to cause the observed queueing at 200 concurrency.

events.message: Root cause: Synchronous PBKDF2 (200k iterations) blocks the event loop, causing tail latency for all requests including GET /me

thread_pool_offload: Offload synchronous PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 computations to a thread pool using asyncio.to_thread() (Python 3.11+), keeping 200k iterations and identical hash format. The event loop stays free to serve GET /me and other requests while login/register/password-change await the offloaded work.

candidate.name: thread_pool_offload
candidate.strategy: Offload synchronous PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256 computations to a thread pool using asyncio.to_thread() (Python 3.11+), keeping 200k iterations and identical hash format. The event loop stays free to serve GET /me and other requests while login/register/password-change await the offloaded work.
candidate.expected_effect: Eliminates event-loop blocking by moving CPU-bound PBKDF2 off the main thread. App CPU remains high but distributed across threads; tail latency for all endpoints drops to near p50 levels. GET /me p99 should fall well below 50 ms because fast DB queries no longer queue behind synchronous hashing.
candidate.risks: Requires Python 3.11+ (asyncio.to_thread). Thread pool adds modest overhead (~0.1 ms per call) and increases memory slightly. If the thread pool saturates (many concurrent logins), requests will queue at the executor rather than blocking the event loop—still a latency improvement but could need tuning. Must ensure telemetry spans still measure PBKDF2 time correctly (they do, inside the offloaded function).

events.message: reduce_iterations: Reduce PBKDF2 iteration count from 200,000 to 10,000 (20× faster per call) while keeping the same algorithm and hash format. Existing stored hashes carry their own iteration count, so verification remains compatible; new hashes use the lower iteration count.

candidate.name: reduce_iterations
candidate.strategy: Reduce PBKDF2 iteration count from 200,000 to 10,000 (20× faster per call) while keeping the same algorithm and hash format. Existing stored hashes carry their own iteration count, so verification remains compatible; new hashes use the lower iteration count.
candidate.expected_effect: Each PBKDF2 call takes ~2 ms (p50) instead of ~38 ms, reducing app CPU load proportionally. Event-loop blocking becomes negligible; GET /me p99 drops below 50 ms. Throughput increases because login/register/password-change spend far less time in CPU-bound work.
candidate.risks: Security margin decreases: 10k iterations is below modern recommendations (OWASP suggests 600k+ for PBKDF2-SHA256). An attacker with DB access can brute-force passwords 20× faster. This fix trades security for latency and should only be used if the threat model accepts it or if a pepper/secret is added separately (not in this change).

events.message: concurrency_semaphore: Limit concurrent PBKDF2 operations to a fixed small number (4) using an asyncio.Semaphore. Requests acquire the semaphore before running PBKDF2, so at most 4 synchronous hashing calls run at once; others wait asynchronously without blocking the event loop. Keeps 200k iterations and identical hash format.

candidate.expected_effect: Caps event-loop occupancy from PBKDF2 to ~4 concurrent calls. With p50 ~38 ms per call, the event loop spends at most ~150 ms per scheduling quantum on hashing, leaving ample time for GET /me and other fast requests. Tail latency for all endpoints drops sharply; GET /me p99 falls below 50 ms. App CPU stays high but no longer saturates the loop.
candidate.risks: Under burst login traffic, requests queue at the semaphore (async wait), adding queueing delay to login/register/password-change. This is acceptable for those endpoints but must be monitored. The semaphore value (4) assumes ~4 CPU cores; if the container has fewer cores, reduce it. Telemetry spans still measure PBKDF2 time correctly inside the critical section.
